A.explanation: With $m \approx 1500 \text{ kg}$ and $v = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, $p = mv \approx 3 \times 10^{4} \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ and $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \approx 3 \times 10^{5} \text{ J}$.

B.explanation: Kinetic energy is reasonable but momentum of $5 \times 10^{6} \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ would need a mass of about $250000 \text{ kg}$, far heavier than a car.

C.explanation: Momentum is reasonable but kinetic energy of $2 \times 10^{7} \text{ J}$ would need a mass of about $100000 \text{ kg}$ at $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: Both values are about 100 times too large and imply a lorry-like or larger mass of order $10^{5} \text{ kg}$.

hints: Start by estimating a reasonable mass for a car in kg - about $1000 \text{ kg}$ to $1500 \text{ kg}$ - combined with the given $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ speed.
Recall $p = mv$ for momentum in $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ and $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ in $\text{J}$, so $E_k$ should equal $pv/2$.
Calculate $mv$ and $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ with your estimated mass and reject any table row where the two values imply very different masses.
walkthrough: Estimate the car mass as $m \approx 1000$ to $1500 \text{ kg}$, a standard order-of-magnitude for a car, with $v = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ given.
Use momentum $p = mv$. For $m = 1500 \text{ kg}$, $p = 1500 \times 20 = 30000 \text{ kg m s}^{-1} = 3 \times 10^{4} \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
Use kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. For the same mass, $E_k = 0.5 \times 1500 \times 20^2 = 0.5 \times 1500 \times 400 = 3 \times 10^{5} \text{ J}$.
Check consistency with $E_k = pv/2$: $3 \times 10^{4} \times 20 / 2 = 3 \times 10^{5} \text{ J}$, so the pair matches the same mass and speed.
Values of order $10^{7} \text{ J}$ or $10^{6} \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ would require $m = p/v$ or $m = 2E_k/v^2$ of order $10^{5} \text{ kg}$, which is not a car. This is option A
